```{r}
library(adempR)
```

This vignette covers the data-generating side of a study: the generator
object, scenario designs given as a table, helpers for correlated
covariates, calibration of model parameters to a target, contamination
and plasmode data, and the three ways adempR reduces Monte Carlo error
(common random numbers, antithetic pairs and control variates).

## The generator object

A plain function `function(scenario, context)` is enough for most
studies. `sim_generator()` wraps it with a check of impossible scenarios,
a version label, declared dependencies and packages (all part of the
fingerprint of the data), a description for the protocol, and a `record`
function that stores realized properties of each data set.

```{r}
gen <- sim_generator(
  function(scenario, context) {
    x <- rbinom(scenario$n, 1, 0.5)
    data.frame(x = x, y = rnorm(scenario$n, scenario$effect * x))
  },
  check = function(scenario) if (scenario$n < 4) stop("need at least 4 observations"),
  record = function(data, meta) c(treated = mean(data$x)),
  description = "two arm trial with normal outcomes")
gen$description
```

The recorded values come back as `records` in `sim_results()` and are
summarized by `sim_diagnose()`, so a mechanism that drifts from its
intended targets (realized censoring, events, balance) is visible.

## Scenario designs from a table

A full factorial grid comes from `sim_scenarios()`. A design that is not
a grid (a fractional design, a list of configurations taken from the
literature) is given as a data frame, one row per scenario.

```{r}
design <- data.frame(n = c(20L, 50L, 200L), effect = c(0.8, 0.5, 0.2))
sc <- sim_scenarios_table(design)
as.data.frame(sc)
```

## Correlated covariates

`sim_check_matrix()` verifies that a correlation or covariance matrix is
symmetric and positive semidefinite, and reports the smallest
eigenvalue when it is not, before anything is simulated.

```{r}
sigma <- matrix(c(1, 0.6, 0.6, 1), 2)
sim_check_matrix(sigma)
try(sim_check_matrix(matrix(c(1, 0.9, 0.9, 0.9, 1, -0.9, 0.9, -0.9, 1), 3)))
```

`sim_rmvnorm()` draws multivariate normal vectors, and `sim_rcopula()`
draws variables with arbitrary margins joined by a Gaussian copula, given
as quantile functions.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
x <- sim_rmvnorm(1000, c(0, 0), sigma)
round(cor(x), 2)
d <- sim_rcopula(1000, list(age = function(p) qnorm(p, 60, 10),
                            smoker = function(p) qbinom(p, 1, 0.3)), sigma)
round(cor(d, method = "spearman"), 2)
```

Inside a generator these use the stream the execution layer assigned, so
they are reproducible like any other draw.

## Calibrating parameters to a target

A target such as an event proportion of 20% or a censoring proportion of
30% is reached by solving for a parameter on a large calibration sample.
The result reports the achieved value and its Monte Carlo SE, so the
calibration error is known; plug the solved value into the scenario.

```{r}
cal <- sim_calibrate_intercept(0.2, function(n) 0.8 * rnorm(n), n = 1e5, seed = 1)
cal[c("intercept", "achieved", "achieved_se")]
cens <- sim_calibrate_censoring(0.3, function(n) {
  sim_rweibull_ph(rnorm(n), lambda = 0.1, shape = 1.5)$event_time
}, horizon = 10, seed = 1)
cens[c("rate", "achieved", "minimum")]
```

## Contamination and plasmode data

`sim_contaminate()` replaces a proportion of values with draws from a
wider distribution and marks which values were replaced, for studies of
robustness.

```{r}
set.seed(4)
y <- sim_contaminate(rnorm(100), prop = 0.1, scale = 10)
sum(attr(y, "contaminated"))
```

`sim_plasmode()` resamples the rows of a real data set and optionally
replaces the outcome with one simulated from a known model, so the
covariate structure is realistic and the truth is known.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
pm <- sim_plasmode(mtcars, n = 50, outcome = function(d) {
  rbinom(nrow(d), 1, plogis(-1 + 0.5 * d$am + 0.02 * (d$hp - 150)))
})
head(pm[, c("am", "hp", "y")], 3)
```

## Data identity

Every committed replication stores a checksum of its data set
(`data_md5` in the replication table). The same function is exported, so
a data set regenerated elsewhere can be compared with the stored one.

```{r}
adempR_data_md5(data.frame(y = 1:3))
```

## Common random numbers

With `common`, scenarios that agree on the named factors draw the same
random numbers. A contrast between scenarios that differ only in other
factors, such as the effect size, then has much less Monte Carlo error.

```{r}
crn <- sim_study("crn", scenarios = sim_scenarios(n = 30L, effect = c(0, 0.5)),
  generate = sim_generator(function(scenario, context) {
    rnorm(scenario$n, scenario$effect)
  }, common = "n"),
  estimands = list(sim_estimand("mean", sim_truth_exact(function(scenario) scenario$effect))),
  methods = list(mean = function(data) sim_estimate("mean", mean(data))))
run_crn <- sim_run(crn, replications = 50, seed = 1, path = tempfile("adempR-run-"))
```

## Antithetic pairs

With `antithetic = TRUE`, replications 2k - 1 and 2k share one data
stream and the second uses the antithetic draws (`context$antithetic` is
`TRUE` there). The pair is the independent unit: every MCSE in
`sim_summarise()` comes from the pairs (a closed form for measures that
are means, a delete-one-pair jackknife otherwise), and the `n_units`
column gives the number of pairs. `sim_summarise_antithetic()` reports
the gain over independent replications.

```{r}
anti <- sim_study("anti", scenarios = sim_scenarios(n = 20L),
  generate = sim_generator(function(scenario, context) {
    z <- rnorm(scenario$n)
    exp(if (isTRUE(context$antithetic)) -z else z)
  }, antithetic = TRUE),
  estimands = list(sim_estimand("mean", sim_truth_exact(function(scenario) exp(0.5)))),
  methods = list(mean = function(data) sim_estimate("mean", mean(data))))
run_anti <- sim_run(anti, replications = 40, seed = 1, path = tempfile("adempR-run-"))
sim_summarise_antithetic(run_anti, "bias")[, c("method", "value", "mcse", "pairs", "variance_ratio")]
```

For proportions such as coverage, pairs whose two members agree can make
every pair mean equal; the MCSE is then 0 but the proportion is not
known exactly. The summary marks such cells as `boundary` and reports an
exact interval built from the number of independent pairs.

## Control variates

A quantity recorded for each data set whose expectation is known exactly
can reduce the Monte Carlo error of a correlated measure. Here the
sample mean of the data is recorded; its expectation is 0.

```{r}
cv <- sim_study("cv", scenarios = sim_scenarios(n = 20L),
  generate = sim_generator(function(scenario, context) rnorm(scenario$n),
                           record = function(data, meta) c(xbar = mean(data))),
  estimands = list(sim_estimand("mean", sim_truth_exact(function(scenario) 0))),
  methods = list(trimmed = function(data) sim_estimate("mean", mean(data, trim = 0.2))))
run_cv <- sim_run(cv, replications = 60, seed = 2, path = tempfile("adempR-run-"))
sim_control_variate(run_cv, "xbar", control_mean = 0, measure = "bias")[,
  c("method", "value", "mcse", "value_adjusted", "mcse_adjusted", "variance_ratio", "status")]
```

The adjustment is made only when every generated data set contributes:
after failed fits the control mean on the remaining data sets is unknown,
and the row gets status `selected` with no adjusted value.
